clauses.clause: Engage in spoken or written dialogue as an author and audience.
clauses.note: Students engage in structured partner discussions, speaking and listening to each other.

clauses.clause: Make intentional connections within texts.
clauses.note: Students discuss and role-play events from one text, but no explicit within-text connection task is directed.

clauses.clause: Make intentional connections between texts.
clauses.note: Only a single text is used; there is no comparison or connection across texts.

clauses.clause: Make intentional connections beyond texts to other knowledge or experiences.
clauses.note: Students discuss their own experiences of sunrise, connecting beyond the text.

verdicts.evidence:
- Gather students together whole group. Tell them that they just finished role-playing what the boy in Summer Sun Risin' experiences when the sun is rising. They now get to talk with a partner about what they experience when the sun is rising. Define experience (to feel or know).
- Tell students they are going to discuss their experience when the sun is rising with a pinky partner. Remind them that they used this protocol in Module 1 and review as necessary, using the Pinky Partners anchor chart. (Refer to the Classroom Protocols document for the full version of this protocol.)
- -Guide students through the protocol to discuss their experience when the sun is rising.
- -As students talk, circulate and listen in. Take note of the ideas students are sharing and target a few students to share out with the whole group. Consider documenting progress toward SL.1.1 using the Speaking and Listening Checklist.
- -Remind students to make a bridge with their arms after both partners have shared.
- -Gather students back together and invite a few students to share with the whole group.
verdicts.rationale: Students engage in partner dialogue and connect the text’s theme to their own experiences, but there is no multi-text comparison and no explicit task to make within-text connections.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text
verdicts.standard_raw_text: Engage in written or spoken dialogue as author and audience for a variety of tasks and purposes, making intentional connections within, between, and beyond texts.

clauses.clause: Provide feedback to others in discussions and shared projects.

verdicts.evidence: Invite students to turn and talk to an elbow partner: 'How will you show respect during our Role-Play protocol?' ... If productive, cue students to listen carefully and seek to understand: 'Who can tell us what your classmate said in your own words?'
verdicts.rationale: Students contribute ideas, listen to others, and provide feedback during structured discussions and collaborative activities.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text

clauses.note: Students discuss and role-play what each character (boy, mother, Pa, sun) is saying and doing.

clauses.note: Students act out and discuss beginning events from the text.

clauses.clause: Identify dialogue used to craft a story.
clauses.note: Students think about what characters might say, but do not identify dialogue in the text.

verdicts.evidence:
- Referring to the Role-Play Protocol anchor chart, explain the steps:
- -Point to the image of the book. Tell students they will listen to a certain part of the text again. (Example: Today students will listen to the beginning events.)
- -Point to the image of the two people talking. Tell students that with their partners, they will think and talk about what each character is saying and doing. (Example: One partner could be the boy, and the other partner could be the boy's mother.)
- -Point to the image of the director's slate. Tell students that when they hear, 'Action!' they will take on the role of their character and act out that part of the text as you read it aloud. (Example: On pages 3-4, students might role-play the boy being awakened by his mother.)
verdicts.rationale: Students identify characters and major beginning events through discussion and role-play. The lesson does not have students identify the setting or dialogue from the text.
